endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: (c) Any vendor-applied constraints on the foundation model's behavior specific to the healthcare deployment context.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether contractual disclosure of escalation triggers, halt conditions, and reversibility makes agentic AI safer, and no study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation rests on a single framework endorsement whose wording addresses vendor-applied model constraints in general rather than these three specific terms.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the opaque-agent hazard. Under GRADE conventions this is a case of no direct evidence. The single endorsement is expert opinion, and its text asks for disclosure of vendor constraints on the foundation model, which only indirectly covers escalation triggers, halt conditions, or reversibility.

The CHAI governance playbook states that health systems should obtain disclosure of vendor-applied constraints on model behavior specific to the health care deployment. This supports disclosure as a contracting norm. The playbook language does not name escalation triggers, automatic halts, or reversal of agent actions, so the recommendation extends the endorsed text rather than restating it.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare deployments with and without contractually documented escalation, halt, and reversibility terms and measure outcomes such as time to detect and reverse erroneous agent actions, the rate of agent errors reaching patients, and the share of vendor-disclosed triggers that function as described when audited. Descriptive work documenting how often opaque agent behavior has impeded oversight or reversal would also establish the size of the hazard.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, so there is no evidence from Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy settings. Health systems serving these patients cannot tell from this evidence whether escalation triggers route patients to human staff who speak their language, or whether halt conditions account for the documentation gaps and resource limits common in safety-net settings.
